newsitem.title: USA: Clinton intervenes in Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton intervenes in Hebron talks.

text.p: The White House said on Monday that President Bill Clinton had intervened in long-running Israeli-Palestinian negotiations on Hebron as the State Department said more work was needed to nail down an accord.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton discussed the Hebron talks by telephone with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday.
Clinton called Mubarak "to exchange views with him on the status of the dialogue" and get Mubarak's insights "into the thinking of those who are negotiating," McCurry said.
Egypt has blamed Israel for the tortoise-like pace of the talks, but some Israeli officials say Cairo is putting pressure on the Palestinian negotiators to stall.

An Israeli handover of 80 percent of Hebron has seemed within reach many times in recent months but concerns for the security of the West Bank town's 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs -- along with other issues -- have delayed an agreement.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai predicted the elusive Hebron deal -- which Palestinian officials had earlier said could be reached on Monday -- would be signed on Tuesday.

The latest progress follows a compromise reached on Sunday, during a lightning mediation mission by Jordan's King Hussein, for Israel to complete three troop withdrawals from still-occupied West Bank areas by mid-1998.

McCurry said Clinton had received regular reports on the talks from U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross, deputy national security adviser Samuel Berger and others, and had "offered some thoughts" on how to resolve differences that have been stalling an agreement.

Cautioning reporters against being "excessively forward-leaning", McCurry said: "We are not encouraging people to leap to exuberant degrees of optimism. This is a process that requires hard work. Some progress has been made but there are differences that remain between the parties."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said later: "Despite the good work by Dennis Ross today, there is no deal yet and there remains the need for additional movement and additional work by both the Israelis and Palestinians before there can be a deal."

Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who asked Ross to call off a plan to return to the United States on Sunday evening, would "evaluate on a day-by-day basis" how long Ross should stay in the region, Burns said.

Israeli ambassador to the United States Eliahu Ben Elissar predicted eventual success. "It will be signed. If not today, it will be signed tomorrow, if not tomorrow, it will be signed the day after tomorrow," he told a meeting of the international Jewish organisation B'nai B'rith in Washington.
Christopher said on Monday that Ross, who has been the target of some criticism in recent weeks, had been asked to stay on in the second Clinton administration which starts next week.

"It is great news that the President and Secretary-designate (Madeleine) Albright have asked him to remain," he said in a luncheon speech to the Conference of Presidents of Major Jewish Organisations.

Some Palestinian officials have accused Ross of favouring Israel in the Hebron talks -- charges rejected by the State Department. And last month, U.S. syndicated columnists Rowland Evans and Robert Novak said a move was afoot to replace him as front-line negotiator with Richard Holbrooke, architect of the Bosnia peace accord. U.S. officials denied that report.
